Understand the project, then present it

A learning notebook • updated 12 November 2026 • current progress and next evidence pathways The research goal is to find natural compounds with herbicidal properties and eventually compare their toxicity with conventional herbicides. This notebook explains the work already completed, why each step matters, what each result means, and what you can responsibly tell your professor. Start here: read the current-progress chapters A–I first. Historical models classify selection groups, and a later model compares reviewed source cohorts. Separate experimental activity fits were also attempted, but they transferred poorly to new studies. External EPA predictions have been collected; their separate analysis is the next planned component. No validated general efficacy, safety or binding predictor has been established. Code is hidden by default so you can focus on the explanations and results; use the editor to inspect the calculations. Use this as a tutorial, not a script to memorize. Read the explanations, change the controls, and answer the practice questions aloud before looking at the suggested answers. Figures and tables load the saved local results; this notebook performs no acquisition, model fitting, approval, or scientific-file edits.

A practical study route

Time available What to do
15 minutes Read the current-progress opening, A–C, H–I, and the new-paper results
45 minutes Read A–I, then add sections 4–14 and the threshold exercise
90–120 minutes Work through everything, inspect individual errors, and rehearse the questions
The exported HTML loads Marimo frontend assets from a CDN. For use without internet, run the locally served notebook with the installed analysis environment. The live notebook has Python-backed controls. The accompanying HTML is a static reading copy with the default results. The opening update includes the 12 November experiments and the new modeled-evidence plan. Later sections retain the human-adopted 11 November checkpoint and older method examples. They are labeled as historical material so different questions are not confused.

A. Two kinds of evidence, and two research tracks

Your professor wants two evidence pathways wherever they are useful: Pathway A: experimental evidence. Someone tested the compound and measured a response. We still need to know the species, dose, time, chemical form and other conditions. Pathway B: estimates from an outside model. A tool such as EPA TEST uses chemical information and earlier training data to estimate a result. This can cover compounds without a direct measurement. It is still an estimate. Possible pathway C, later: combine them carefully. First finish and evaluate A and B separately. Then ask whether combining them improves results on a genuinely held-out experimental test set. These pathways do not replace our two research tracks:
Research track Main question How A and B could help
Track 1: non-target toxicity How do natural products and herbicides differ in toxicity? Analyze measured toxicity and externally predicted toxicity in separate comparisons
Track 2: plant activity and chemistry What do natural compounds with plant effects look like? Use measured plant responses; separately examine external non-target toxicity estimates for those compounds
A predicted rat LD50 is not a label for herbicidal activity. If we cannot find a suitable external plant-activity model, we should say so. We can still study predicted non-target hazard alongside measured plant efficacy. When we say “experimental-only,” we mean the outcome labels come from experiments. Structure counts and fingerprints are calculated descriptions of molecules. Predicted logP and other estimated properties must be labeled as estimates, not measured properties. If both inputs and outcomes must be experimentally measured, that needs a stricter, smaller dataset.

How to read that chart

Each test paper was kept out of training. The earlier paper tests used the original pooled dataset. The new radish test used the original 73 compounds for training and 20 new labeled compounds for testing. Training sizes therefore differ; this is not one common test set. The plant assays also differ. In the new radish test there were two high responses and 18 low responses. All three fixed models missed both high responses: F1 was zero. A model can correctly label many low-response compounds and still fail to find the high-response compounds we care about. A second check removed training molecules sharing a scaffold with the new paper. It removed 21 He compounds because they shared a broad benzene scaffold with test catechol. Morgan models then found both positives but predicted far too many positives overall: precision was only about 0.13 for logistic regression and 0.11 for the forest. That is unstable behavior, not a selected improvement. We did not keep changing thresholds until this paper looked good. These results support a clear next step: better data coverage and carefully defined targets, plus the separate external-model pathway. They do not support using the pooled model to rank new bioherbicides.

What the latest weights, forest and shuffled-label checks mean

In the pooled activity experiment, more chlorine as a fraction of the formula had a positive logistic weight, while oxygen count had a negative weight. These are associations in this particular pooled dataset. Chemistry and source paper are linked here, so the weights do not show that adding chlorine causes activity or removing oxygen improves a herbicide. The forest's OOB F1 was about 0.744, compared with about 0.680 in scaffold-held-out testing. OOB leaves out a molecule for each tree; it can still train on related molecules. The two scores therefore answer different questions. The most influential bit in the OOB shuffle check reduced F1 by about 0.040 on average. A fingerprint bit is a hashed structural signal, not automatically one unique chemical group. The spread across repeat shuffles is not a p-value. We also attempted 20 shuffled-label checks for each representation. Shuffling breaks the chemistry-to-label relationship. Only 10 runs could be scored for each representation; the other 10 lacked the required scaffold/class support and stayed unsupported. Formula PCA's actual F1 lay inside the scored shuffled range. Morgan PCA's actual F1 was above the largest of the 10 scored shuffled results. This is a small exploratory check, not adjusted for testing many models, and it did not repair poor transfer to new papers. The tables below use saved outputs. No new model is fitted here. Later sections 12–14 teach the earlier selection-model diagnostics; those use different labels and should not be mixed with these activity results.

data.text/markdown:
D. What the new literature added

The broader search transcribed 304 plant-response observations and 59 other-endpoint observations from seven papers. A separate full 27-compound study added 324 observations: two plant species × three doses × two endpoints × 27 compounds. These are repeated conditions, not 324 different molecules. In each species' 100 µM root-growth policy, that new study had 2 high, 18 low and 7 intermediate responses. The low-response examples covered nine scaffold groups; the two high responses covered only two. That still does not support our five-fold activity classifier for the individual assay policy. “Low response” here means little inhibition under a stated test. It can include growth stimulation. It does not mean the compound has no biological effect or is safe. The 27 database structure mappings are provisional, and their natural-origin labels remain unknown in this new experiment. Six pairs compared a parent molecule with an O-methylated version. In simple terms, an O-methyl group replaces a hydroxyl hydrogen with a methyl group. Some pairs, especially chrysin and pinocembrin at 100 µM, showed stronger mean inhibition after this change. Other pairs were less consistent. The measurements have uncertainty, so these are ideas for further study, not a rule that methylation always improves activity.
